n: Years have passed, and Joshua is now old. God gently tells him the work is far from finished — much land is still unconquered. The second half of the book turns from conquest to inheritance.

f.w: there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed

n: Remaining lands include all the Philistine territory and the region of the Geshurites in the south.

f.g: Sea peoples who settled on the southern coast around this time.
Here a southern people near Philistia, different from Geshur in the north.

n: The five Philistine city-states — Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron — each ruled by a “lord,” stretched from the brook of Egypt northward.

f.g: Probably the Wadi of Egypt (Wadi el-Arish), Canaan’s southwest border.
Hebrew seranim — a special Philistine title for rulers.

n: Also unconquered: Canaanite land in the north from Mearah near Sidon to Aphek.

f.g: The Phoenicians of the coastal city of Sidon.

n: And the Gebalites, all Lebanon from Baal-gad under Hermon to Lebo-hamath — the northern boundary of the promised land.

f.g: People of Gebal (Byblos), a Phoenician port.

n: God promises to drive out these peoples himself. Joshua’s task is to assign the land by lot now, in faith that it will be possessed.
The land west of the Jordan is to be divided among nine and a half tribes.

f.w: the nine tribes, and the half tribe of Manasseh

n: The other two and a half tribes already received land east of the Jordan from Moses.
The eastern territory began at Aroer on the Arnon gorge and included the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon.

f.g: Where the famous Moabite Stone (Mesha Stele) was discovered in 1868.

n: It included all the cities once ruled by Sihon from Heshbon, up to the Ammonite border.
Also Gilead, the borders of Geshur and Maacah, Mount Hermon, and Bashan.

f.g: A town on Bashan’s eastern frontier.

n: All of Og’s kingdom in Bashan, last of the Rephaim, conquered under Moses.
An honest note of incomplete obedience: the Geshurites and Maacathites were not driven out and still lived among Israel. David later married a Geshurite princess, mother of Absalom.
Levi alone received no territory; their portion was the fire offerings of the Lord.

f.w: the sacrifices of the LORD God of Israel made by fire

n: Now the allotment of Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, is described clan by clan.
Reuben’s territory began in the south at the Arnon and included the Medeba plateau.

f.w: the city that is in the midst of the river
f.g: A town in the Arnon valley.

n: Towns include Heshbon, Dibon, and places named for Baal — remnants of Canaanite and Moabite worship in the region.
More towns on the tableland.
Towns including Kiriathaim and Sibmah, later famous for vineyards.
Beth-peor, near where Moses was buried; the slopes of Pisgah; and Beth-jeshimoth.
The region once ruled by Sihon, who was allied with Midianite chieftains killed in Israel’s war against Midian.

f.w: the princes of Midian, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba

n: Balaam, the hired diviner who tried to curse Israel and then led them into sin at Peor, was killed among them.

f.w: Balaam also the son of Beor

n: The Jordan formed Reuben’s western border.
Next, Moses’ allotment to the tribe of Gad.
Gad received Jazer, the cities of Gilead, and part of the former Ammonite lands up to Aroer near Rabbah.

f.g: The Ammonite capital — modern Amman, Jordan.

n: From Heshbon north to Ramath-mizpeh and from Mahanaim, where Jacob met angels.
Gad also held the eastern Jordan valley, including Succoth, up to the Sea of Galilee.
Summary of Gad’s inheritance by clans.
Then the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan.
Their land ran north from Mahanaim through all Bashan, including the sixty towns of Jair.
Half of Gilead, plus Og’s royal cities, went to the clans of Machir, Manasseh’s son.
These were the lands Moses distributed on the plains of Moab before he died.
Repeated for emphasis: Levi had no land, for the Lord God himself was their inheritance — a richer gift than any territory.

f.w: the LORD God of Israel was their inheritance
